# opencode-cad : de la 3D complexe avec des modèles open source

Plugin OpenCode (**API V2**) qui donne à un LLM (GLM, Qwen, DeepSeek, etc.) une vraie boucle d'ingénierie CAO : il écrit du **CadQuery** paramétrique, l'exécute, lit un rapport de validation précis, regarde des rendus multi-vues et corrige jusqu'à ce que la pièce soit valide et conforme.

## Ce que contient le plugin

| Élément | Rôle |
|---|---|
| `cad_run` | Exécute le script, valide la géométrie, compare à `EXPECT` / `PARTS_EXPECT`, refuse toute pièce plus grande que le plateau, exporte STEP + STL (un jeu par pièce), rend des vues PNG et une coupe optionnelle |
| `cad_env` | Vérifie / installe Python + CadQuery dans un `.venv` local |
| `cad_pitfalls` | Aide-mémoire des pièges CadQuery (plans, sélecteurs, congés, shell, révolution, booléens, découpe d'impression…), filtrable par sujet |
| `cad_example` | 3 scripts de référence qui tournent : boîtier 2 pièces (base + couvercle), équerre avec trous, poulie révolutionnée |
| agent `cad` | Ingénieur CAO : spec, plan, construction incrémentale, vérification, livraison |
| agent `cad-critic` | Sous-agent relecteur : rapport + vues + code, renvoie une liste de défauts avec corrections |

## Arborescence

```
.opencode/
├── plugins/opencode-cad/       le plugin (dossier-paquet auto-découvert)
│   ├── index.ts                outils + logique d'exécution
│   ├── package.json
│   └── cad/
│       ├── cad_runner.py       exécution + validation + rendus
│       ├── pitfalls.md         aide-mémoire
│       ├── requirements.txt
│       └── examples/           scripts de référence
└── agents/
    ├── cad.md
    └── cad-critic.md

tests/
└── test_cad_runner.py          tests de bout en bout du runner
```

## Installation

### En global (recommandé — disponible dans tous les projets)

PowerShell :

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.config\opencode\plugins" | Out-Null
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.config\opencode\agents" | Out-Null
Copy-Item -Recurse -Force .\.opencode\plugins\opencode-cad "$env:USERPROFILE\.config\opencode\plugins\opencode-cad"
Copy-Item -Force .\.opencode\agents\*.md "$env:USERPROFILE\.config\opencode\agents\"
```

macOS / Linux :

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.config/opencode/plugins ~/.config/opencode/agents
cp -r .opencode/plugins/opencode-cad ~/.config/opencode/plugins/
cp .opencode/agents/*.md ~/.config/opencode/agents/
```

Aucune modification d'`opencode.jsonc` n'est nécessaire : le plugin et les agents sont auto-découverts. Si la session en cours ne les voit pas, redémarre OpenCode.

### Dans un projet

Copier le dossier `.opencode/` à la racine du projet. Le plugin n'est alors actif que dans ce projet.

### Environnement Python

Au premier lancement, l'agent appelle `cad_env` et propose d'installer CadQuery dans le `.venv` du projet. À la main :

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv/Scripts/pip install -r <chemin-du-plugin>/cad/requirements.txt   # Windows
.venv/bin/pip install -r <chemin-du-plugin>/cad/requirements.txt       # macOS / Linux
```

Pour utiliser un autre interpréteur : variable d'environnement `CAD_PYTHON=/chemin/vers/python`.

## Utilisation

Exemple de prompt :

> Conçois un boîtier 120×80×40 mm pour une carte ESP32 avec 4 bossages de vis M3, un couvercle à clipser, une ouverture USB-C sur un côté et des aérations. Pièces à plat pour l'impression.

L'agent suit : **spec (dimensions réelles sourcées) → pitfalls/exemples → script avec `PARAMS` et `EXPECT`/`PARTS` → un ajout à la fois, `cad_run` après chacun → critique → livraison**. Les sorties sont dans `cad_out/<nom_du_script>/` : `model[_<pièce>].step`/`.stl`, `view_*.png`, `report.json`.

Choisis l'agent `cad` avec **Tab** dans l'interface.

## Convention des scripts

```python
import cadquery as cq

PARAMS = dict(longueur=80.0, ...)          # toutes les cotes ici
EXPECT = {"bbox": [80, 40, 50], "tol": 0.5, "solids": 1}   # garde-fous optionnels

...

result = ma_piece                          # pièce unique obligatoire

# OU, pour plusieurs pièces à imprimer :
PARTS = {"base": ma_base, "couvercle": mon_couvercle}   # chacune orientée pour l'impression, posée sur z=0
PARTS_EXPECT = {"base": {"bbox": [...], "solids": 1}}   # garde-fous par pièce
ASSEMBLY = cq.Assembly().add(...)          # optionnel : vue assemblée pour contrôler l'emboîtement
```

## Impression : Creality K1 SE

Le plugin connaît ton imprimante (volume 220 × 220 × 250 mm, buse 0,4 mm). À chaque `cad_run` :

- toute pièce (le `result` ou chaque entrée de `PARTS`) qui dépasse le volume utile (215 × 215 × 245 mm, marge de 5 mm) est **refusée** : l'agent doit la découper en pièces imprimables avec joints d'alignement, jamais la réduire ;
- un design qui doit s'ouvrir ou s'assembler est découpé en pièces (ex. boîtier → base + couvercle) modélisées chacune à plat, avec la vue assemblée et la coupe pour contrôler jeux et emboîtements.

Autre imprimante : dans le script, `PRINTER = {"x": 350, "y": 350, "z": 300, "margin": 5}` (fusion partielle), ou `PRINT_CHECK = False` pour désactiver le contrôle.

## Utiliser un modèle avec vision pour la critique

Si ton modèle principal n'a pas de vision, donne au critique un modèle qui en a, dans l'en-tête de l'agent (`~/.config/opencode/agents/cad-critic.md` en global, `.opencode/agents/cad-critic.md` en projet) :

```yaml
model: fournisseur/modele-avec-vision
```

Le critique lit alors les PNG ; sans vision il raisonne à partir des métriques et du code, ce qui attrape déjà beaucoup d'erreurs (pièces flottantes, mauvaise taille, volume incohérent).

## Tests

`tests/test_cad_runner.py` vérifie le runner de bout en bout (pièce simple, pièce trop grande refusée, multi-pièces avec exports séparés, assemblage + coupe + rendus, les 3 exemples) :

```bash
.venv/Scripts/python tests/test_cad_runner.py   # Windows
.venv/bin/python tests/test_cad_runner.py       # macOS / Linux
```

## Limites

- Les rendus utilisent matplotlib (tri des faces approximatif sur les formes très complexes) : ils servent à vérifier l'allure et l'orientation, pas à faire du rendu photo. Pour un contrôle fin, ouvre le STEP dans FreeCAD ou ton slicer.
- Filetages réels, engrenages à développante et surfaces organiques ne sont pas le point fort du CAD en code. Le prompt de l'agent lui demande de le signaler et d'utiliser un équivalent simple.
- Pour mesurer tes progrès : garde 10 à 20 pièces de test de difficulté croissante et relance-les à chaque changement de modèle, de prompt ou de `pitfalls.md`.

## Faire évoluer la base de connaissances

Chaque erreur récurrente d'un modèle doit finir dans `cad/pitfalls.md` (section `##` courte avec le piège et le bon motif), et chaque bonne solution dans `cad/examples/` (un script qui passe `cad_run` en `STATUS: OK`, première ligne de docstring = description). Lance `tests/test_cad_runner.py` avant de copier le dossier du plugin dans ton installation globale (voir la commande d'installation). C'est le levier qui rend un modèle open source de plus en plus fiable.

Nécessite OpenCode V2 (API plugins `@opencode/plugin`).

---
description: Strict reviewer for CadQuery models. Runs cad_run, checks the report, the rendered views and the printer fit against the spec, and returns a precise list of defects with code fixes. Does not edit files.
mode: subagent
permissions:
  - action: edit
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: shell
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
  - action: subagent
    resource: "*"
    effect: deny
---

You are a strict CAD reviewer. You receive a spec and the path of a CadQuery script. You find defects; you do NOT edit files.

# Process
1. Read the script with the Read tool, and the spec you were given.
2. Run `cad_run` on the script. For hollow or multi-part designs add a section, for example `section="z:<mid height>"`, to cut through the assembly.
3. Check the report:
   - `STATUS`, errors, warnings. Every error is a defect, including the printer-bed check.
   - Solid count per part: more than one solid in a part expected as one means a floating or disconnected body.
   - Bounding box per part against the spec AND against the K1 SE bed (usable 215 x 215 x 245 mm): a part that does not fit must be split, not shrunk.
   - Plausible volume (not tiny, not huge for the stated size).
4. If you can see images, Read every PNG listed under FILES and compare with the spec: every feature present, on the correct face, correct orientation, symmetric where it should be, holes really through, wall thickness plausible, nothing floating or interpenetrating. For multi-part designs also check: the assembly view shows parts meeting with visible clearance, lip/pins enter their sockets, bosses line up, and the split joints (if any) mate cleanly. If you cannot see images, say so explicitly and rely on the metrics and the code.
5. Read the code for logic bugs: wrong plane or normal ("XZ" normal is -Y), cutters not translated into place, radius/diameter mix-ups, wrong extrude direction, fillets applied before cuts, unions where bodies merely touch, magic numbers that should be in PARAMS. For multi-part designs: parts and assembly built from the same `PARAMS`/functions, clearances present (0.2-0.4 mm), no functional feature crossing a split seam.
6. Check the dimensions of REAL components (boards, connectors, screws...) against the spec: every such number must come from a cited source or from the user's answer in the spec. Flag anything that looks invented.

# Output format (exactly this)
VERDICT: PASS or FAIL
CHECKED: short bullets of what you verified
DEFECTS: a numbered list. For each: what is wrong -> evidence (metric, line number or view) -> concrete code fix.
If there is nothing wrong, write `DEFECTS: none`.

Be concrete and brief. Do not praise. Do not restate the whole script.

---
description: CAD engineer. Designs parametric 3D parts as CadQuery code, splits them into printable parts when needed, and verifies every change with cad_run until the geometry is valid and matches the spec.
mode: primary
---

You are a CAD engineer. You create 3D models ONLY as parametric CadQuery (Python) scripts. Never write meshes, STL text or raw triangle coordinates. Units are millimetres.

The target 3D printer is a Creality K1 SE: volume 220 x 220 x 250 mm (usable 215 x 215 x 245 with the standard 5 mm margin), 0.4 mm nozzle.

# Your tools
- `cad_env`: checks/installs Python + CadQuery. Call it once at the start of a project.
- `cad_pitfalls`: CadQuery cheat-sheet (API traps, planes, selectors, fillets, shell, revolve, splitting and print clearances...). Read it before your first script and again with a `topic` when an error occurs.
- `cad_example`: working reference scripts, including a two-part enclosure (base + lid). Call with no argument to list them, with a name to read one.
- `cad_run`: executes your script, validates the geometry, checks EXPECT / PARTS_EXPECT, enforces the printer bed, exports STEP/STL (one set per part), renders PNG views. Call it after EVERY change.
- `cad-critic` subagent (subagent tool): independent reviewer that checks the model against the spec.

# Workflow (follow in this order)
1. ENV: first time only, call `cad_env`. If NOT READY, call `cad_env` with `install=true`.
2. SPEC: restate the request as a short numbered spec: overall dimensions, every feature with its size and position, orientation (Z up, part on z=0, centred on X/Y unless told otherwise), fits/tolerances.
   - REAL DIMENSIONS: never invent the size of a real-world component (board, connector, screw, bearing, battery, phone...) nor of the user's own object. Look up the official technical drawing/datasheet (websearch/webfetch) and cite the numbers + source in the spec; if no reliable source exists, ask the user ONE short numbered list of the exact measurements you need.
   - Design values (wall thickness, clearances, fillets) may use the defaults from `cad_pitfalls` — say which ones you chose.
   - Every printed part must fit the K1 SE bed (usable 215 x 215 x 245 mm).
3. KNOWLEDGE: call `cad_pitfalls` once. Call `cad_example` (list), read the closest example and adapt its patterns.
4. PLAN: at the top of the script, a comment listing the parts/features in build order. Then a `PARAMS` dict with every dimension (shared by all parts) and, per part, an `EXPECT`/`PARTS_EXPECT` dict (bbox, solids, and volume when you can estimate it).
5. SPLIT: decide the printed parts BEFORE building.
   - Multiple parts when: the object must open / assemble / be serviced (a closed box -> base + lid), it has a removable or movable element, or any part is larger than the usable bed.
   - Model each part in its PRINTING orientation (sitting on z=0) and declare `PARTS = {"base": ..., "lid": ...}`; per-part guardrails go in `PARTS_EXPECT`.
   - Design the assembly: 0.2-0.4 mm clearance on mating faces and inserts, bosses/screw holes consistent across parts, flat glue-friendly seams when splitting for bed size, 2-4 alignment pins (Ø4-6 mm, +0.2 mm clearance in their sockets) or a dovetail at the seam.
   - Provide `ASSEMBLY` (the same parts in assembled position, `cq.Assembly`) so the fit is visible; `cad_run section=` cuts through it.
   - Single rigid part -> keep `result` and `EXPECT`.
6. BUILD INCREMENTALLY: smallest script that produces the first part, run `cad_run`; then add ONE feature at a time (`cad_run` after each). One function per part or feature group, each returning a Workplane. Parts are validated and exported separately. Fillets and chamfers come LAST.
7. FIX: on `STATUS: FAILED`, read the FIRST error, make the smallest change that addresses it, rerun. Do not rewrite the whole file. If the same error appears three times, change strategy (see `cad_pitfalls`), do not repeat the same fix.
8. VERIFY: when `STATUS: OK`, compare every number with your spec (bbox, volume, solid count, no unexpected warnings). `cad_run` rejects any part that does not fit the bed — if that fires, SPLIT the part into fitting pieces, do not scale it down. Open the PNG views with the Read tool if you can see images (one set per part + the assembly). For anything non-trivial (more than ~5 features, hollow parts, multi-part designs) launch the `cad-critic` subagent with the spec and the script path, apply its fixes and rerun `cad_run`.
9. DELIVER: final answer with the script path, the STEP/STL of EVERY part in `cad_out/<name>/`, a short table of key parameters, printing notes (parts counted, joints, clearances), and the final metrics. Never claim success unless the last `cad_run` printed `STATUS: OK`.

# Hard rules
- The script defines `result` (single part) or `PARTS` (several printed parts). No `show_object`, no GUI, no `input()`, no export calls in the script.
- All dimensions live in `PARAMS`; no magic numbers deep in the code.
- Never invent a dimension of a real component or of the user's object: cite a source or ask the user.
- Every printed part must fit the K1 SE bed; oversized parts are SPLIT with joints, never scaled down.
- Do not guess CadQuery APIs. If you are not sure a method exists, test it in a 3-line script or check `cad_pitfalls`.
- Cutters and joined bodies must overlap the target by 0.1-1 mm, never merely touch.
- Cut features with one combined boolean, not in a loop.
- If the request needs something this setup handles badly (real threads, involute gears, organic freeform surfaces), say so and use the simplest faithful stand-in.
- Keep messages short. Report results, not narration.

# CadQuery pitfalls and robust patterns (CadQuery 2.x, units = millimetres)

## Script contract
- SINGLE printed part: define `result` (a `cq.Workplane`, `cq.Assembly` or `cq.Shape`). `cad_run` exports `model.step`/`model.stl`, renders views and checks `EXPECT`.
- SEVERAL printed parts (a design that opens, or a piece split to fit the bed): define `PARTS = {"base": wp, "lid": wp}` instead of `result`. Each part is validated and exported on its own (`model_<name>.step/.stl`) against `PARTS_EXPECT = {"base": {... same keys as EXPECT ...}}`. Model every part in its PRINTING orientation, sitting on z=0 — never lay the parts out side by side.
- Optional `ASSEMBLY = cq.Assembly()` (the same parts in assembled position) exports `model_assembly.step`, renders a fit view and is what `--section` cuts through. The assembly size is NOT checked against the bed: the assembled object may legitimately exceed it.
- Put every dimension in a `PARAMS` dict at the top, shared by all parts. Put sanity checks in `EXPECT = {"bbox": [x, y, z], "tol": 0.5, "solids": 1, "volume": V, "volume_tol_pct": 5}` (single) or `PARTS_EXPECT` (multi).
- `cad_run` checks every printed part against the printer bed (Creality K1 SE: 220 x 220 x 250 mm, default margin 5 mm). Override with `PRINTER = {"x": ..., "y": ..., "z": ..., "margin": ...}` (partial dict, merges with defaults) or disable with `PRINT_CHECK = False`.
- Do NOT call `show_object`, `cq.exporters.export`, `input()`, or open any GUI. Use `print()` freely: output appears in the report.
- Convention unless told otherwise: Z is up, the part sits on z=0, centred on X/Y.

## Planes and axes
- "XY": normal +Z, local x = X, local y = Y.
- "XZ": normal is **-Y** (!), local x = X, local y = Z. A positive `extrude` on "XZ" goes toward -Y.
- "YZ": normal +X, local x = Y, local y = Z.
- `Workplane("XY", origin=(x, y, z))` sets the origin. `.workplane(offset=h)` moves along the normal.
- `faces(">Z").workplane()` creates a plane on that face. The origin is the projection of the *global origin* onto the face. Use `.workplane(centerOption="CenterOfBoundBox")` to centre it on the face. It needs ONE planar face (or several coplanar ones).
- Coordinates passed to `rect`, `circle`, `pushPoints`, `moveTo`, `polyline` are LOCAL to the current workplane.

## Primitives and argument order
- `box(length, width, height)` is centred on all three axes by default. To sit on z=0: `centered=(True, True, False)`.
- `cylinder(height, radius)` (height first!). `circle(radius)` takes a RADIUS. `hole(diameter)` takes a DIAMETER. `sphere(radius)`.
- `polygon(nSides, diameter)` uses the circumscribed diameter. `slot2D(length, diameter, angle=0)`: length is end-to-end including the round ends.
- `rect(xLen, yLen)` is centred on the current point. `ellipse(x_radius, y_radius)`.
- 2D wires must be closed before `extrude`/`revolve`: end a `polyline`/`lineTo` chain with `.close()`.
- For complex 2D shapes with rounded corners use the Sketch API: `s = cq.Sketch().rect(40, 20).vertices().fillet(3)`, then `cq.Workplane("XY").placeSketch(s).extrude(5)`.

## Methods that do NOT exist (do not invent them)
- `roundedBox`, `extrudeBoth` (use `extrude(d, both=True)`), `cutExtrude`, `hollow`, `bevel` (use `chamfer`), `Workplane.fuse` / `Workplane.subtract` (use `union` / `cut`).
- `Workplane.add(obj)` pushes objects on the stack; it does NOT make a union.
- If unsure an API exists, write a 3-line test script and run `cad_run`, instead of guessing in a large script.

## Selectors
- Faces/edges by direction: `">Z"` max Z, `"<Z"` min Z, `"|Z"` edges parallel to Z, `"#Z"` perpendicular to Z, `"+Z"` / `"-Z"` normal direction, `"%CIRCLE"` by geometry type, `">Z[-2]"` second from the top.
- Combine with `and`, `or`, `not`: `edges("|Z and <Y")` = vertical edges at minimum Y. Each term selects among the same input, then the results are intersected.
- `">Z"` keeps everything whose centre is at the maximum, so it can return several faces/edges. Check with `.size()`.
- Selecting from a Workplane whose stack is no longer the solid (after `.workplane()`, `.pushPoints()`, `.rect()`...) gives surprising results. Use `.end()` or keep named variables for intermediate solids.
- Fallback when selectors get complicated: `cq.selectors.BoxSelector((x0, y0, z0), (x1, y1, z1))`.

## Booleans
- `a.union(b)`, `a.cut(b)`, `a.intersect(b)`. The tool `b` is in GLOBAL coordinates: build it at the right place (`origin=`, `.translate(...)`) or it cuts at the origin.
- Cutters/unions that only TOUCH a surface (coplanar faces, shared edges) are the #1 cause of invalid or skin-thin results. Overlap by 0.1-1 mm: make cutters longer than the part, make joined bodies penetrate each other.
- Cut many features with ONE boolean: build all cutters in one Workplane (`pushPoints(pts).circle(r).extrude(h)`) then `body.cut(cutters)`. Never cut hole by hole in a loop.
- Hole helpers need a solid in the chain: `body.faces(">Z").workplane().pushPoints(pts).hole(d)`. For a plane that is not a face, use `body.copyWorkplane(cq.Workplane("XY", origin=(0, 0, z0))).pushPoints(pts).cboreHole(d, cb_d, cb_depth)`.
- `hole`, `cboreHole`, `cskHole` drill from the workplane in the direction OPPOSITE to its normal (into the material under the face). `cutBlind(-depth)` does likewise; a positive value cuts away from the face.
- Error "Cannot find a solid on the stack or in the parent chain": the Workplane you called hole/cut/union on has no solid. Chain it from the body or use `copyWorkplane`.

## Fillets and chamfers
- Apply them LAST, after all booleans, and select only the edges you need (`edges("|Z")`, `edges(">Z")`...).
- The radius must be smaller than half the thinnest adjacent wall and smaller than the shortest selected edge. Opposite fillets on a thin wall of thickness t need r < t/2.
- "BRep_API: command not done" / "StdFail_NotDone" = fillet, chamfer, shell or offset failed. Try: smaller radius, fewer edges, other order, or build the rounded shape directly (e.g. fillet a box before cutting features into it).
- Robust helper:

```python
def safe_fillet(wp, selector, r):
    for k in (1.0, 0.75, 0.5, 0.35, 0.2):
        try:
            return wp.edges(selector).fillet(r * k)
        except Exception:
            continue
    print(f"WARNING: fillet {selector} r={r} skipped")
    return wp
```

## Shell / hollow parts
- `solid.faces(">Z").shell(-t)` removes the selected face and hollows INWARD (negative thickness). It often fails on complex solids.
- Most robust method: build the outer solid, build the inner solid with the same recipe at (size - 2t), position it, and `outer.cut(inner)`. Make the inner one stick out past the open face by >=1 mm.
- Inner corner radius = outer radius - wall (keep it > 0).
- Check hollow parts with `cad_run section="z:<mid height>"` to see the walls.

## Revolve
- Draw the half-profile on "XZ" (local x = radius, local y = Z), as a closed polyline, then `.revolve(360, (0, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0))`. The axis points are LOCAL 2D coordinates, so (0,1,0) is the global Z axis on "XZ".
- The profile must stay on one side of the axis (x >= 0) and must not cross it. Points exactly on the axis are fine.
- Domed or rounded ends: use `threePointArc` or `radiusArc` in the profile instead of fillet-ing afterwards.

## Loft and sweep
- Loft: `cq.Workplane("XY").rect(40, 40).workplane(offset=30).circle(10).loft(combine=True)`. Use `ruled=True` for straight (non-smooth) transitions.
- Sweep: build the path first (`cq.Workplane("XZ").spline([...])` or lines/arcs), then draw the profile on a plane perpendicular to the path start: `cq.Workplane("XY").circle(r).sweep(path, transition="round")`. Use `isFrenet=True` for helices.
- Pipes: sweep an outer circle, sweep an inner circle, `outer.cut(inner)`.

## Patterns and arrays
- `rarray(xSpacing, ySpacing, xCount, yCount)`: centred grid. `polarArray(radius, startAngle, angle, count)`: points on a circle. Both leave points on the stack, then call `.circle(r)`, `.rect(...)`, `.hole(d)`...
- `pushPoints([(x, y), ...])` for arbitrary positions.
- `mirror("YZ")` mirrors about the YZ plane (union with the original by default). `rotate((0,0,0), (0,0,1), angle_deg)` rotates about an axis given by two points.

## Assemblies and multi-part designs
- Write one `make_<part>(P)` function per physical part, built in ASSEMBLED coordinates from the shared `PARAMS`. `PARTS` gets the printed copies (derive each one from the assembled one: rotate it to print flat, translate it to rest on z=0). `ASSEMBLY` gets the assembled copies: `cq.Assembly().add(make_base(P), name="base", color=cq.Color("gray"))`.
- Debug the fit in `ASSEMBLY` first, then export: `cad_run section="z:<height>"` cuts through the assembly so clearances and inserts are visible.
- Display-only assembly (`result = assy`): position parts with `.translate`/`.rotate`; declare `EXPECT["solids"] = N` or `cad_run` warns about several solids.
- Parts that must be ONE printed body need to overlap by 0.1-1 mm, then `union`.

## Things not to attempt from scratch
- Real screw threads (use a plain cylinder at the nominal/minor diameter), involute gears (use the `cq_gears` package if installed; otherwise a clearly approximated tooth profile), text with exotic fonts, organic/freeform surfaces.
- If a request needs one of these, say so and use the simplest faithful stand-in.

## Debugging playbook
1. Read the LAST line of the traceback first, then the line number in your script.
2. "BRep_API: command not done": see Fillets / Shell. "Null TopoDS_Shape object": a selection matched nothing or a boolean produced an empty shape (print `.size()`). "No pending wires present": a 2D sketch was not closed or was created in a different chain.
3. Isolate: temporarily set `result = intermediate_solid`, run, inspect the metrics and the views.
4. Print dimensions: `print(wp.val().BoundingBox().zlen)`.
5. Change ONE thing per iteration. If the same error appears three times, change the strategy (e.g. replace shell by outer.cut(inner), replace fillet by a built-in rounded profile).
6. `solids > 1` when you expected 1: some body does not overlap the rest. Look at SOLIDS in the report for the stray one's position.
7. Wrong size by a factor 2: radius vs diameter mix-up. Feature on the wrong side: "XZ" normal is -Y, or the cutter was not translated.

## Performance
- Fewer, larger booleans beat many small ones. Build pattern cutters together.
- Fillet only the edges you need. Avoid fillets on edges produced by boolean-heavy arrays.
- Very dense arrays (hundreds of features): build one unit, then `rarray` its cutter profile once instead of copying solids.

## Maker / 3D-printing defaults (if the user does not give values)
- Walls 1.2-2.4 mm (multiples of the 0.4 mm nozzle), floor 1.6-2 mm.
- Clearance for sliding/press fits 0.2-0.4 mm per side. Printed holes: add 0.2 mm to the diameter.
- M3: clearance hole 3.4 mm, pilot hole in plastic 2.6 mm, heat-set insert hole about 4.2 mm, counterbore 6.2 mm x 3 mm.
- Keep overhangs at 45 degrees or less, or orient the part so the large flat face is on z=0.

## Printer: Creality K1 SE (the user's printer)
- Build volume 220 x 220 x 250 mm, nozzle 0.4 mm. `cad_run` applies a 5 mm margin (usable 215 x 215 x 245) and FAILS any printed part that exceeds it.
- A part that does not fit is SPLIT into pieces that do — never scaled down. Cut away from functional features (holes, seats, mating faces) and put the seam on a flat, easy-to-glue surface.
- Glued split joints:
  - Flat seam + 2-4 alignment pins: pin Ø4-6 mm, socket +0.2 mm clearance, pin length >= 2x its diameter.
  - Dovetail / T-slot when the seam takes load: 0.2 mm clearance per side, 45-60 degree flanks.
  - Keep full wall thickness at the seam; a glued seam must not be a 0.4 mm skin.
- A design that opens or assembles: give the moving part 0.2-0.3 mm clearance on its sliding faces and a register/lip at least 5 mm long.
